title: Multilevel Marketing: Last Week Tonight with John Oliver (HBO)
summary: A comedy news segment on MLMs argues income comes from recruiting, exponential recruiting exhausts the population, most distributors earn nothing, and volume discounts push stockpiling of unsold product.

assertions.quote: You make a little, not much. Not enough to pay the bills that are wrecking up. You make money from signing people up.
you could only do that 13 cycles and you would exceed the population of the earth.

verdicts.note: Simple arithmetic: five recruits per level exceeds world population by about the fourteenth level, so late joiners cannot build a downline.

assertions.quote: the overwhelming majority of Herbal Life distributors who pursue the business opportunity make little or no money and a substantial percentage lose money.

verdicts.note: Company income disclosures and regulator analyses across many MLMs consistently show the median participant earns under expenses.

assertions.quote: to stay qualified for those higher discounts, you have to keep buying product.

verdicts.note: Inventory loading is a documented feature of many compensation plans and was central to the regulator's complaint cited in the segment.

Many MLMs require or encourage product purchases to maintain rank or compensation eligibility, with a court finding one plan pushed participants to buy hundreds of dollars of product monthly and participants reporting stockpiling to keep rank; the report does not measure whether that product goes unsold.

AARP's consumer advice warns of 'inventory loading' from minimum inventory requirements to stay active or earn commissions, and about one in ten leavers said they were forced to spend more than they wanted to keep membership active.

Taylor found pay-to-play purchase requirements of $50-$500 a month to qualify for commissions and rank advancement in the MLMs he examined, with resale to outsiders only a minor part of sales so the product is mostly consumed or given away.

assertions.quote: New recruits were told, Herbal Life products helped to treat heart disease.

verdicts.note: Undercover recordings and regulator warning letters repeatedly document disease-cure claims by distributors despite company policies.
Taylor warns recruits against promoters' claims that MLM products have magical properties that heal or prevent every disease; an observation from his research, not a measured study.

assertions.quote: explaining one narrow part of their insanely convoluted compensation plan.

verdicts.note: Plans are demonstrably complex and hard for participants to model; whether the complexity is deliberate is inferred rather than shown.

Taylor states the income distribution has been obfuscated by complex compensation plans that are difficult to compare, and that company earnings statistics are laden with obfuscation apparently to avoid revealing the odds; intent is his inference.

assertions.quote: you should know those refunds can be partial or may involve resigning.

verdicts.note: Typical buyback terms deduct restocking fees and apply only on termination, which company policies state.

One quoted disclosure refunds the initial order 100% only if the distributor resigns within 30 days and later orders at 90% only on resignation within a year with unopened product; a single example, but it matches the pattern claimed.

assertions.quote: They've only brought around two dozen pyramid scheme cases against MLMs in the last four decades.

verdicts.note: The count of enforcement actions is low relative to the industry's size and a congressional direct-selling caucus exists.

Taylor reports the FTC admitted prosecuting only 14 MLM companies in ten years and that the DSA lobby got MLM exempted from the Business Opportunity Rule; he also attributes the inaction to victims seldom filing complaints rather than only opacity and political connections.

assertions.quote: active distributors represent only around 36% of total distributors.

verdicts.note: Disclosures routinely exclude inactive or non-earning distributors from the denominator, inflating reported earning rates.

Of 70 disclosures only 11 clearly include all participants; 29 drop everyone who earned no commission and 24 drop participants the MLM deems 'inactive', so at least 75% present a distribution that omits zero-earners.
The FTC found most disclosures leave out or downplay the percentage of participants who made no money while emphasising the high earnings of a few.

Taylor documents that MLM disclosures use only currently active distributors as the base (Nu Skin's actives were 40.71% of distributors of record) and exclude dropouts, which greatly skews success rates in the company's favour.
